summary:
The Kids Internet and Digital Safety Act (KIDS Act) establishes federal requirements for covered online services used by minors, enforced principally by the Federal Trade Commission as violations of rules under Federal Trade Commission Act § 18(a)(1)(B), 15 U.S.C. § 57a(a)(1)(B), with parens patriae civil enforcement by State attorneys general subject to FTC notice, intervention, and federal-action preclusion.

Title I, the SCREEN Act, requires, beginning 1 year after enactment, providers of publicly accessible platforms on which more than one-third of knowingly made-available material is “sexual material harmful to minors” to adopt commercially available technology verification measures, prevent minors from accessing such material, provide notice, address circumvention, minimize transfer/disclosure/retention of verification data, and maintain reasonable data security. It authorizes third-party verification without relieving provider liability, disclaims any requirement to submit government identification, requires FTC consultation, and directs a GAO report within 3 years. It preempts State age-verification requirements for such platforms, with savings clauses for specified State laws.

Title II defines covered platforms and imposes minors’ online-safety obligations. Subtitle A, the Kids Online Safety Act, requires reasonable policies addressing enumerated harms to minors; safeguards and default protective settings for known minors; parental tools, including defaults for known children; reporting mechanisms with substantive responses within 10 days or sooner for imminent threats; disclosures and parental-consent processes; advertising labels for paid endorsements; a prohibition on facilitating advertising of specified illegal or age-restricted products to known minors; and independent annual audits beginning 18 months after enactment with FTC and public reporting. It disclaims any age-gating or age-verification mandate and preempts conflicting State law. Subtitle B, the Safe Messaging for Kids Act, prohibits ephemeral messaging for known minors, prohibits direct messaging for known users under 13, and requires parental direct-messaging controls for known teen users, subject to encryption-preservation rules; it takes effect 180 days after enactment except § 235, which follows the Act’s default effective date. Subtitle C, the SPY Kids Act, effective 90 days after enactment, prohibits market or product-focused research on known minors except for safety/privacy-related improvement or legal compliance.

Title III, the Safer GAMING Act, requires online video game providers to furnish default, most-protective parental communication safeguards for known minor users and tools addressing recommendations, purchases, and time limits, with notice to covered users. Title IV, the SAFE BOTs Act, prohibits false licensed-professional representations by chatbots to known minors, mandates AI and crisis-resource disclosures, and requires policies addressing break prompts after 3 hours and specified harmful content.

Title V mandates FTC, HHS/NIH, and Commerce studies, reports, educational resources, and establishes a Commerce Kids Internet Safety Partnership for 5 years. Section 522 amends subtitle A of the Protecting Children in the 21st Century Act, 15 U.S.C. § 6551 et seq., by replacing §§ 211–214 and 216 with an FTC public-awareness program, 10 years of annual reports, and definitions. Title VI centralizes enforcement, channels constitutional challenges exclusively to the D.C. Circuit with 90- and 60-day limitations periods, preserves COPPA and 47 U.S.C. § 230, protects encryption, bars compelled new age-data collection, includes severability, and sets a default effective date 1 year after enactment.
